job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Olga Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Olga, and thank you for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in electrical power engineering at Ostrava Polytechnic, and I live at home with my parents and my grandmother, about forty minutes by train. I get up at six, help my grandmother with breakfast, and take the early train to lectures on transformers and protection. In the evenings I do the books for my father's electrical contracting firm, which has six electricians and two apprentices. My bachelor's was electrical engineering, and I did an internship with a regional utility and a summer on my father's crews, pulling cable. On Sundays I sing in the church choir, and that's the one place my phone stays in my bag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, good, I never saw the point of all the noise. At home I'd say we'll carry on as we are, a day's work for a day's pay. To the people at church I'd say you can't automate a neighbour who needs the lights fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means I can finish the master's and do what my family expects. I'd work a few years at the utility, learn how real networks are run, then maybe help take over my father's firm. There are always jobs in power, and I'd be one of the ones who gets offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and apply to the utility and two network companies. I'd keep doing my father's books on weekends, as I've done for years. And I'd put a bit of my pay toward my grandmother's care costs, which I've promised my mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I planned for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You do your father's books. Could software take over some of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, I know there are programs. But I like knowing every invoice and who hasn't paid, and my father trusts my handwriting more than a screen. I'm not against new things, I just don't see why I'd change what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything still worry you if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandmother's health, and my father's knees, since he's fifty-eight and still climbing ladders. If he stopped suddenly, the firm would need someone fast, and that someone would be me. That's a worry I can't hand to a computer.

say: I'd say there was never a point to all the noise, and a **day's work** for a day's pay stands.
At church I'd say you can't automate a **neighbour** who needs the lights fixed.
think: I finish the master's, work at the **utility**, and maybe help take over my father's firm.
My real worries are my **grandmother's health** and my father's knees.
do: Apply to the **utility** and two network companies after the degree.
Keep doing my father's **books** and put money toward my grandmother's care.
feel: **Calm**; it's the world she planned for.

fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on family duty and a trade that always has work.
Worries about **ageing relatives**, which no technology removes.
Resists new tools through preference, not hostility.

steps.text: Apply to the regional utility and two network companies
Keep doing the firm's books on weekends
Put money each month toward my grandmother's care costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of change for ordinary people, and it should be handled with care. At church I'd say look after each other and teach your children real skills. At work I'd say let the firms that benefit pay for the retraining, not the workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office side of power engineering shrinks first. Design checks, drawings and reports are thinking work and they'd move to software. Out in the field, though, you still need people with a ladder and a licence, and my father's electricians are not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean toward field-based engineering, on substations and live networks. I'd get my practical licence early, since it's a paper nobody can fake. And I'd ask my father to take on another apprentice, because I believe in training the next one up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I feel steady, but I see people I know having a hard time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the new tools at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm required it, yes, I'd learn. I'd rather watch others use them for a year first. I've seen young engineers trust a program's answer and not notice a wrong cable rating, and that kind of mistake can burn a house down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whom would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Dorota, who works in a bank's back office. Her team shrank twice already, and her manager says more will go. She has a husband and a little boy, and I worry she's the one who pays first.

say: I'd say it's a lot of change and **firms that benefit** should pay for retraining.
At church I'd say look after each other and teach children **real skills**.
think: Design checks and reports are **thinking work** that shrinks first.
Field work with a ladder and a licence stays, so my father's **electricians** aren't worried.
do: Lean toward **field-based** engineering and get my practical licence early.
Ask my father to take on another **apprentice**.
feel: **Uneasy**; she feels steady but sees people she knows struggling.
S1.quote: I've seen young engineers trust a program's answer and not notice a wrong cable rating, and that kind of mistake can burn a house down.
fieldNote: Her view of **training** the next person is both moral and practical.
Resists tools out of **safety** concern, with a concrete fire example.
Worries about her cousin Dorota, whose bank team has shrunk twice.

steps.text: Aim for substation and live-network field engineering roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and that politicians and companies have been careless. I'd say we need families, churches and local groups to look after one another, because governments won't be ready. I'd also say that work gives people dignity and we shouldn't lose that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm afraid. If thinking AI does almost any desk job by 2028, the engineering jobs at the utility are among the first to be reshaped. My father's electricians have about 3 more years, but I'd be the one with the degree and nowhere to put it. I'd worry that my master's was for a world that's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the family firm and make myself useful, with the books, the bids, and the site work. I'd stop the master's after the first year if I had to, and I'd start my practical licence. I'd also keep my savings in cash, because I don't trust anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm frightened, though I'd keep it from my grandmother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the AI tools, given what's at stake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, for the books and the bids, but I'd be doing it with my teeth clenched. I'd test them on old invoices first. If I get a wrong total, I'd go back to the ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my father, I'm coming home to work, and he'd say no, finish your degree. I'd say the degree can wait, the firm can't. We'd argue, and my mother would make tea, and I'd win by saying nothing for a while.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and politicians and companies have been careless.
I'd say **families and churches** must look after one another, because work gives dignity.
think: Utility engineering jobs are among the first to be **reshaped**, and I'd have a degree with nowhere to put it.
My father's electricians have about **3 more years**.
do: Go to the **family firm** and take on the books, bids and site work.
Stop the master's after **year one** if needed and start my practical licence.
feel: **Anxious**, frightened, though she'd hide it from her grandmother.
S2.quote: The degree can wait, the firm can't.
fieldNote: Her answer is the **family firm**, a strong traditional pull in a crisis.
Would use AI for books only with **teeth clenched** and tested on old invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to be sensible, and enough for fools to waste. I'd say we should build apprenticeships, not just more degrees. And I'd tell my church group to make a plan for who helps whom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be nervous. By 2031 I'd be 29, probably married, perhaps with a child, and I'd want the family firm solid. The thinking jobs go first, but we get until about 2034 on hands-on work, which gives my father's crew a little more time than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work at the utility for two or three years, and then join the family firm. I'd save hard and keep my family close, maybe even buy a house near my parents. And I'd learn the new office tools only when the firm needs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. A few years' warning helps, but it also means I can't say I didn't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why anxious, with five years to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my plan relies on things staying put for ten years: the utility, the firm, my husband's job. If the utility cuts engineers in 2030, I'd have two years of experience and a loan for a house. I've seen what happens to people who get caught half-way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the picture look if the date were 2036 rather than 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be calmer, I'd have time to marry, to have a child and to become a proper engineer. Five years feels like the child is born in the middle of it, and I'd prefer the child to be born after I'm settled.

say: Five years is enough to be **sensible**, and enough for fools to waste.
I'd say we should build **apprenticeships**, not just more degrees.
think: By 2031 I'd be **29**, perhaps married with a child, and want the firm solid.
Hands-on work lasts until about **2034**, giving my father's crew more time than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should use it well. I'd say let's put money into apprenticeships and local firms now. And I'd tell my church friends that a good family and a good trade beat any machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be only a bit uneasy. By 2036 I'd be 34, with a family, a proper career, and perhaps the firm in my hands. My father would be nearly seventy, and I'd want to make the firm strong enough to hand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work at the utility to learn the big picture, and join the firm by about 28. I'd marry, have children and save hard. And I'd take on the office tools bit by bit, whenever my father's firm needs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but fine. It's something I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still make you uneasy with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That someone else decides. I don't want a big company or the government to decide how my father's firm lives or dies. I'd want to be at a table where it matters, and I'd vote and join the trade association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your own children about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn something real with their hands, and also to learn to read a contract. Whatever the machines do, they'll need to be able to say no and to know what the paper says.

say: Ten years is long, so let's put money into **apprenticeships** and local firms now.
I'd tell church friends a **good family** and a good trade beat any machine.
think: By 2036 I'd be **34**, with a family and perhaps the firm in my hands.
I'd be uneasy that **someone else decides** how my father's firm lives or dies.
do: Finish the master's, learn at the utility, and join the **family firm** by about 28.
Join the **trade association** and vote in every election.
feel: **Uneasy**, but fine, because she can plan for it.
S4.quote: I'd tell my children to learn something real with their hands, and also to learn to read a contract.
fieldNote: Her unease is about **who decides**, a traditional, local-control concern.

steps.text: Join the family firm by about age 28
Keep working steadily on the firm's books and bids

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one. I'd be caught between a degree I can't use and a family firm that needs help right now. What would help is time, honestly, and steady work for the firms who train apprentices. I'd also like the church and community groups to be allowed to help, with rules that don't squeeze them out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Perhaps that I'm not afraid of change, I'm afraid of change that nobody has taken responsibility for. Someone should be answerable. If a machine makes a mistake, a person should still have to stand in front of the family and say it was their fault.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of change, I'm afraid of change that nobody has taken responsibility for.
portrait: Olga is 24, doing a **master's** in electrical power at Ostrava Polytechnic and living with her parents and grandmother.
She keeps her father's firm's books, sings in a church choir and leans to **family and work** over handouts.
She prefers the familiar, takes few risks and has **never used AI** tools.
She is calm if little changes, but anxious when **time is short** for her marriage and the firm.
Her anchor is the family electrical firm, and she trusts apprenticeships.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because she'd have a degree with nowhere to put it.
whatWouldHelp: More **time**, and steady work for firms that train apprentices.
Rules that let **churches and community groups** help without being squeezed out.
